title: Fully polynomial relative entrywise \(\ell_1\) low-rank approximation
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), is there a deterministic fully polynomial approximation scheme for entrywise \(\ell_1\) low-rank approximation: on every rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), rank bound \(1\leq k<n\), and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), output a rank-at-most-\(k\) factorization with error at most \((1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}_k(A)\) in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\)? This explicitly selected interpretation has a negative resolution under the stated assumption.
why: The question marks a basic computational distinction between least-squares matrix compression and robust entrywise approximation. Its hardness and approximation results explain why provable robust compression requires careful parameter dependence. The selected standard tractability target is settled under its stated complexity assumption and is retained outside the active open-problem benchmark.
status_note: The selected fully polynomial version is resolved negatively assuming P differs from NP, by the published sign-matrix rank-one hardness and its objective gap. Review completed on 13 September 2026. This is a conditional tractability classification, not a proof of P different from NP or a blanket impossibility of fixed-parameter approximation schemes.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 13 September 2026; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

importance.reason: A fundamental tractability boundary for robust low-rank matrix approximation; the historical question led to both rank-one hardness and relative approximation schemes.

sentences: Robust low-rank approximation measures reconstruction error by the sum of absolute entrywise differences.
The source asks for a polynomial-time algorithm returning a rank-k factorization within a factor one plus epsilon of the best such approximation.
This changes the geometry from the squared-error setting where singular values and standard sketching methods are especially effective.
Approximating a sum of row norms is also a different guarantee and does not settle the entrywise objective.
An algorithm or hardness classification would clarify whether near-optimal robust matrix compression admits the same broad computational tractability as classical low-rank approximation.

definitions: For a real matrix \(D\), its entrywise norm is \(\|D\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}|\), not the induced matrix one-norm and not a sum of Euclidean row norms. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(A)=\min_{B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\,\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_1\). This minimum is attained: the rank-at-most-\(k\) set is closed, and bounded objective sublevel sets are bounded in the matrix entries. The algorithm receives the dense matrix as signed binary rational numerators and positive denominators, together with binary encodings of \(n,k\) and \(\varepsilon\). Its output is a pair of rational matrices \(U\in\mathbb Q^{n\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb Q^{k\times n}\), with \(\|A-UV\|_1\leq(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}_k(A)\). Factors need not be nonnegative, orthogonal, sparse, or formed from input rows and columns. Their total encoding length and the time to write them are charged. There are no promises on conditioning or on the optimum; when the optimum is zero the output must reproduce \(A\) exactly. Fully polynomial means that one deterministic multitape Turing machine and an absolute constant \(b\) work for all inputs, with running time \(O((N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)^b)\), where \(N\) is the total input bit length. The exponent is independent of \(k\) and \(\varepsilon\). Here \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decidable in deterministic polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) of languages with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in deterministic polynomial time. The displayed complexity assumption is part of this historical target, not a theorem asserted by the card.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked conditional answer must either construct a scheme with the stated factorization, accuracy and bit running time, or prove that any such scheme would imply P equals NP. The latter implication is the published-hardness consequence relevant to this resolved record. No unconditional proof that P differs from NP, and no existing Lean formalization of the literature proof, is claimed.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s Open Question 2 asks about relative entrywise approximation and also asks whether hardness is known. Its phrase “polynomial time” leaves parameter dependence unspecified, while the comparison algorithm for a weaker row-norm objective treats rank and accuracy as fixed. This card explicitly selects the fully polynomial interpretation and the usual P-versus-NP assumption; it does not attribute those conventions verbatim to the source.

Gillis and Vavasis establish NP-hardness already for rank-one approximation of sign matrices. Their Theorem 2 shows that such inputs have an optimum represented by sign factors, and Theorem 3 establishes the hardness. The resulting discrete objective gap rules out a fully polynomial relative scheme under P different from NP. This consequence uses the approximation gap, not merely a claim that exact optimization is hard.

Song, Woodruff and Zhong give provable approximation algorithms and also an ETH-based obstruction to sufficiently fine inverse-logarithmic relative accuracy, even at rank one. Their results substantially change the state described in the 2014 survey.

Ban, Bhattiprolu, Bringmann, Kolev, Lee and Woodruff give a polynomial-time approximation scheme with a polynomial exponent depending on rank and inverse accuracy. Their stated input model has polynomially bounded integer entries. This positive fixed-parameter result does not have fully polynomial dependence on accuracy and is consistent with the hardness above.

An input with fewer rows than columns, or the reverse, can be embedded into a square matrix by zero padding without changing the best rank-bounded error. The distinction between square and rectangular matrices therefore does not remove the cited hardness.

Absolute entrywise error is a standard way to reduce sensitivity to sparse large corruptions, but robustness changes the computational geometry. The completed historical record distinguishes a fast approximation at fixed parameters from a single scheme with a uniform polynomial degree.

resolution.result: No deterministic fully polynomial relative scheme unless P equals NP, already at rank one.
resolution.verification: Checked the sign-matrix optimum theorem, its discrete gap and the NP-hardness theorem. A scheme at inverse-polynomial accuracy would recover the integral optimum by exact rational evaluation and rounding. No unconditional separation or Lean formalization is claimed.

review_outcome.reason: The explicitly selected fully polynomial tractability target is settled negatively under P different from NP; the fixed-parameter interpretation also has a published PTAS in its stated input model.
